The composite indicator for "career impact" was obtained by adding the ratios of six log-transformed bibliometric indicators (Table 1), not excluding self-citations (Ioannidis et al., 2020, p. 2).
Notably, Ioannidis et al. (2020) are among the few prominent representatives in bibliometrics who favor composite indicators, particularly in the context of a measurement perspective.

Furthermore, Ioannidis et al. (2020) describe their composite indicator as a quantification of a scientist’s career-long impact; thus, this is a form of scholarly scientific impact that can be interpreted (at least partly) as intellectual influence (Garfield, 1970; Moed, 2017b).

Hence, our first aim is to address the gap in the scientometric literature by providing a complete argument for why a reflective measurement model is appropriate for an author-level impact composite such as the one proposed by Ioannidis et al. (2020).

Our thorough investigation of Ioannidis et al.’s (2020) composite in a selective sample of eminent researchers revealed that some indicators do not fit well, that a more parsimonious composite could reasonably replace the original composite, and that such a composite displays excellent reliability.
As compared to the original Ioannidis et al. (2020) composite, excluding NCS was the main reason for decreasing the intercorrelations with all composites used in this work below unity (see Table 6).
